newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thailand sees 10 pct exports growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Thailand sees 10 pct exports growth in 1997.

text.p: Thailand's Commerce Minister Narongchai Akarasanee said on Monday he was confident that the country's exports growth this year would meet a target of at least 10 percent.

He told reporters that the current slide of the Thai baht against the surging dollar could benefit Thailand's exports but such a trend was not desirable because it could affect the country's overall economic stability.

Thailand was projected to export 1.56 trillion baht of goods this year, or attain 10 percent exports growth over last year, the minister said. The maximum the ministry hopes to achieve is 15 percent exports growth.
"It is important that we must meet our target on exports, otherwise the GDP growth will rely on the domestic economy only and won't be able to grow above five or six percent," the minister said.

Narongchai said exports growth, which contracted last year, would benefit from a recovery of the world economy, forecast by the IMF at 4.1 percent, and his ministry's measures to facilitate exports by restructuring the tax system.
He said Thailand targeted Southeast Asian markets as its top priority. Overall, industrial goods were expected to be the nation's biggest foreign exchange earners.

"However, exports at this moment are not only about growth. It's about stability as well. As long as we cannot convince investors and currency punters that we can narrow the c/a deficit, the baht will continue to come under pressure," he added.

The minister stressed that baht stability was crucial to the competitiveness of Thai exports and the overall economy. "The easing baht against the dollar generally can boost export revenue. But that is only one side of it," he said.
The weak baht, hit by attacks from offshore speculators and a surging U.S. dollar, had led to tight liquidity, forcing the Thai central bank to maintain high interest rates, he said.
These high rates would affect industry and result in higher costs of production as a negative side effect.
"It is important that we must restore baht stability," Narongchai said.
